Flagship Research Project

Computational FSI Simulation of Bat Flight

Investigating how membrane perforations affect aerodynamic performance through fluid-structure interaction modeling at the University of Tennessee Space Institute.

At a Glance

Role: Research Intern · Extended and validated an existing FSI codebase

Advisor: Dr. Esteban Cisneros-Garibay, UTSI

Duration: June 2026 – present

Stack: Firedrake, PETSc, Python, Gmsh, VisIt, Slurm/HPC, Git

Problem Statement

Bat wings are thin, flexible membranes that frequently sustain tears and perforations from encounters with vegetation, predators, or disease (such as white-nose syndrome). Despite these injuries, bats often continue flying — suggesting their flight mechanics are somewhat tolerant to membrane damage.

Understanding exactly how perforations affect lift, drag, and energy expenditure requires high-fidelity computational models that couple the fluid flow with the structural response of the membrane — a fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problem.

Methodology

The simulation framework uses the finite element method viaFiredrake (built on PETSc) for spatial discretization. The approach evolved through several stages:

2D Model → 3D Extension

Initial work used a 2D flow field coupled with a 1D elastic filament to understand the basic coupling mechanics. This was then extended to 3D flapping bat-wing geometries with membrane perforations — a significant step up in computational complexity.

Mesh Generation

Wing geometries are meshed in Gmsh. To create anatomically accurate models, I extracted wing-boundary coordinates directly from a bat photograph and used them to construct the computational mesh.

Numerical Methods

The linear systems are solved using Krylov subspace methods (GMRES) with preconditioning, including algebraic multigrid where appropriate. Key numerical fixes I implemented:

  • Fixed a one-sided traction integral to a two-sided formulation for correct force coupling across the membrane
  • Added a Gaussian envelope function to suppress non-physical oscillations at wing tips
  • Debugged mesh inversion issues that arose during large membrane deformations

Validation

The solver was validated against the Blasius flat-plate solution — an analytical benchmark for boundary layer flow over a flat surface. This confirmed that the velocity profiles and skin friction coefficients matched theory to within acceptable tolerances.

Energy-Expenditure Model

Beyond the fluid-structure coupling, I integrated an energy-expenditure model that accounts for flow temperature, thermal balance, and mechanical power output. This allows parametric studies connecting perforation geometry to the total energetic cost of flight.

Current & Future Work

  • Two-way FSI coupling: Full bidirectional feedback between fluid forces and membrane deformation
  • Leaky-filament conditions: Modeling flow through perforations with varying sizes and locations
  • Parametric studies: Systematic investigation of how perforation geometry maps to aerodynamic degradation
